title: Two-Heap Median Finder
summary: Tracking a running median from a data stream by balancing a max-heap and a min-heap — O(log n) insert, O(1) median read, no sorted structure needed.

slides.markdown:
Finding the median of a fixed array is easy (sort, take the middle). Finding the median of a **stream** — where new values keep arriving and you need the current median after every one — is a different problem, and re-sorting on every insert is O(n log n) per element, far too slow.

The two-heap trick gets insert down to O(log n) and median lookup down to O(1): split the stream into a max-heap holding the smaller half of values and a min-heap holding the larger half, kept balanced in size. The median is then always sitting at the top of one or both heaps — no scan, no sort, just a peek.

slides.subTitle: A max-heap (lower half) and a min-heap (upper half)
slides.markdown:
The core idea: maintain two heaps that together hold every value seen so far, split down the middle. The **lower half** — all values less than or equal to the current median — lives in a **max-heap**, so its largest element (the boundary closest to the median) is instantly accessible at the top. The **upper half** lives in a **min-heap**, so its smallest element (the other boundary) is instantly accessible at the top.

This is a deliberate choice of heap type per half: you always want fast access to whichever element is **closest to the median** in each half, which means the max of the lower half and the min of the upper half — exactly what each heap type gives you for free at its root.

slides.sectionTitle: The two-heap split after inserting a stream
slides.markdown: <<< Image: a sequence of numbers being inserted one at a time into two heaps drawn side by side — a max-heap on the left holding the smaller half of values seen so far, a min-heap on the right holding the larger half — with the boundary between them updating as new numbers arrive and cross from one heap to the other to keep both halves balanced in size >>>

slides.subTitle: Sizes differ by at most one, lower-half max ≤ upper-half min
slides.markdown:
Two invariants must hold after every insert, not just "eventually": the two heaps' **sizes** differ by at most one (so the median is always derivable from just the two roots, never requiring a scan), and every value in the max-heap is ≤ every value in the min-heap (so the split boundary is genuinely where the median sits, not an arbitrary partition).

Both invariants together guarantee: if the heaps are equal size, the median is the average of both roots; if one heap has one extra element (by convention, usually the max-heap), the median is simply that heap's root. Maintaining both invariants on every insert — not just the size one — is what the next two slides cover.

slides.subTitle: Push to one heap, then transfer the root if sizes drift
slides.markdown:
```python
import heapq

lo = []  # max-heap, stored as negated values
hi = []  # min-heap

def add_num(num):
    heapq.heappush(lo, -num)                    # always insert into lo first
    heapq.heappush(hi, -heapq.heappop(lo))       # then move lo's max into hi...
    if len(hi) > len(lo):
        heapq.heappush(lo, -heapq.heappop(hi))   # ...and pull it back if hi overflowed
```

The "push into lo, immediately move the max into hi, then possibly move it back" dance looks redundant but is what guarantees **both** invariants simultaneously: the transfer through `hi` ensures the new value ends up on the correct side relative to the existing split (since `hi`'s pop-then-compare naturally sorts it against the boundary), and the final rebalance step keeps the size difference at most one.

slides.subTitle: In O(1) from the two heap roots
slides.markdown:
```python
def find_median():
    if len(lo) > len(hi):
        return -lo[0]              # lo has the extra element: it's the median
    return (-lo[0] + hi[0]) / 2.0  # equal sizes: average both roots
```

Both heap roots are O(1) to peek, so the entire median lookup is O(1) — no traversal, no recomputation, just reading two array indices (accounting for the negation on the max-heap side). This is the entire payoff of maintaining the two invariants on every insert: the O(log n) insert cost buys an O(1) query forever after, versus re-sorting for O(n log n) every single time the median is needed.

slides.sectionTitle: Inserting into the wrong heap first
slides.subTitle: And skipping the cross-check against the other root
slides.markdown:
```python
# BUG: pushes directly into whichever heap "seems right" by comparing
# to the current median, but never cross-checks against the actual boundary
def add_num_wrong(num):
    if not lo or num <= -lo[0]:
        heapq.heappush(lo, -num)
    else:
        heapq.heappush(hi, num)
    # missing: any rebalancing step at all
```

Without the transfer-then-rebalance dance from the correct implementation, this version can violate the size invariant (nothing keeps the two heaps within one element of each other) **and** the ordering invariant (a value can land in the wrong heap if the comparison against a stale root is wrong at the boundary) — both silently, with `find_median()` then returning a value that isn't actually the median, no error raised. The size-check-only approach that skips the actual transfer through the other heap is the most common shortcut people try, and it's specifically the ordering invariant it fails to guarantee.

slides.sectionTitle: Two-heap median vs a sorted-insert structure
slides.subTitle: Simpler code, same O(log n) insert
slides.markdown:
| | Two-heap median | Sorted-insert structure (BST/skip list) |
|---|---|---|
| Insert | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| Median read | O(1) | O(log n) (walk to the middle) or O(1) with an augmented size-tracking BST |
| Code complexity | two heaps, careful rebalancing | requires an ordered structure, possibly augmented with subtree sizes |
| Supports arbitrary rank queries | no — only the median | yes, with the right augmentation |

Both get insert to O(log n). The two-heap approach wins decisively on **median-read speed** (true O(1), no walk) and is usually simpler to implement correctly than an augmented BST. A BST-based structure wins if you need more than the median — arbitrary percentile or rank queries — which two heaps fundamentally can't answer; they only ever expose the two boundary values, nothing else.

slides.subTitle: Sliding-window median, and why removal breaks the simple two-heap trick
slides.markdown:
A natural follow-up: "running median over the last k elements" (a sliding window) instead of the whole stream. This needs **removal** — evicting the element that just fell outside the window — and that's exactly where the simple two-heap trick breaks down: a plain heap has no efficient way to remove an arbitrary (non-root) element, only ever the root.

The practical fix mirrors the decrease-key workaround from the priority-queues topic: **lazy deletion**. Mark the evicted value as "stale" (via a count in a hash map) rather than physically removing it from whichever heap it's in, and when a root happens to be a stale value during a rebalance or a median read, pop and discard it before using the next root instead. This keeps both heaps' true, |non-stale| sizes balanced conceptually, while their raw sizes (including stale entries) may drift — a real added layer of bookkeeping beyond the basic two-heap median.
